"executive_summary": "This study utilizes the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS) to investigate the radio properties of 31 blazars detected by the EGRET instrument on the Compton Gamma-Ray Observatory. The VIPS survey provides uniform, high-resolution VLBI imaging of flat-spectrum sources down to a flux limit of 85 mJy at 5 GHz, covering a region of approximately 5700 square degrees. By comparing the morphological and polarization properties of these gamma-ray selected sources against the broader VIPS population of 1127 sources, the authors test hypotheses regarding the physical mechanisms driving gamma-ray emission. The analysis reveals that EGRET-detected blazars exhibit distinct characteristics compared to the general radio-loud population. Specifically, these sources show a statistically significant tendency toward higher core fractions, higher brightness temperatures, and potentially larger jet opening angles. While the sample size for detailed component analysis is small (only 4 sources permitted unbiased jet opening angle calculations), the aggregate data supports the hypothesis that gamma-ray loud blazars possess systematically larger Doppler factors. This suggests that the gamma-ray emission arises from regions oriented at smaller angles to the line of sight compared to the radio-selected population. The study also notes a lack of correlation between radio and gamma-ray flux densities at lower flux levels, implying that radio brightness alone is not a reliable predictor of gamma-ray activity. These findings have implications for future observations by the GLAST satellite (now Fermi), suggesting that selection strategies based on core fraction and brightness temperature may be more effective than simple flux cuts for identifying gamma-ray loud blazars.",

summary.title: Characteristics of EGRET Blazars in the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS)
summary.authors: G. B. Taylor, S. E. Healey, J. F. Helmboldt, et al.
summary.executive_summary: This study utilizes the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS) to investigate the radio properties of 31 blazars detected by the EGRET instrument on the Compton Gamma-Ray Observatory. The VIPS survey provides uniform, high-resolution VLBI imaging of flat-spectrum sources down to a flux limit of 85 mJy at 5 GHz, covering a region of approximately 5700 square degrees. By comparing the morphological and polarization properties of these gamma-ray selected sources against the broader VIPS population of 1127 sources, the authors test hypotheses regarding the physical mechanisms driving gamma-ray emission. The analysis reveals that EGRET-detected blazars exhibit distinct characteristics compared to the general radio-loud population. Specifically, these sources show a statistically significant tendency toward higher core fractions, higher brightness temperatures, and potentially larger jet opening angles. While the sample size for detailed component analysis is small (only 4 sources permitted unbiased jet opening angle calculations), the aggregate data supports the hypothesis that gamma-ray loud blazars possess systematically larger Doppler factors. This suggests that the gamma-ray emission arises from regions oriented at smaller angles to the line of sight compared to the radio-selected population. The study also notes a lack of correlation between radio and gamma-ray flux densities at lower flux levels, implying that radio brightness alone is not a reliable predictor of gamma-ray activity. These findings have implications for future observations by the GLAST satellite (now Fermi), suggesting that selection strategies based on core fraction and brightness temperature may be more effective than simple flux cuts for identifying gamma-ray loud blazars.

There is no direct correlation between radio flux density and gamma-ray flux density at lower flux levels.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study utilizes the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS) to investigate the radio properties of 31 blazars detected by the EGRET instrument on the Compton Gamma-Ray Observatory. The VIPS survey provides uniform, high-resolution VLBI imaging of flat-spectrum sources down to a flux limit of 85 mJy at 5 GHz, covering a region of approximately 5700 square degrees. By comparing the morphological and polarization properties of these gamma-ray selected sources against the broader VIPS population of 1127 sources, the authors test hypotheses regarding the physical mechanisms driving gamma-ray emission. The analysis reveals that EGRET-detected blazars exhibit distinct characteristics compared to the general radio-loud population. Specifically, these sources show a statistically significant tendency toward higher core fractions, higher brightness temperatures, and potentially larger jet opening angles. While the sample size for detailed component analysis is small (only 4 sources permitted unbiased jet opening angle calculations), the aggregate data supports the hypothesis that gamma-ray loud blazars possess systematically larger Doppler factors. This suggests that the gamma-ray emission arises from regions oriented at smaller angles to the line of sight compared to the radio-selected population. The study also notes a lack of correlation between radio and gamma-ray flux densities at lower flux levels, implying that radio brightness alone is not a reliable predictor of gamma-ray activity. These findings have implications for future observations by the GLAST satellite (now Fermi), suggesting that selection strategies based on core fraction and brightness temperature may be more effective than simple flux cuts for identifying gamma-ray loud blazars.

Research Context
At high galactic latitudes at least ∼70% of the sources seen by the Compton Gamma-Ray Observatory (CGRO) EGRET instrument are identified with blazars These blazars exhibit ﬂat radio spectra, rapid variability, compact cores with one-sided parsec-scale jets, and superluminal motion in the jets The identiﬁed EGRET blazars display a number of interesting radio properties However, in consideration of a larger sample (taken at 2 and 8 GHz) Piner et al. (2007) ﬁnd no signiﬁcant diﬀerence between the jet velocities of EGRET and non-EGRET blazars It still is unclear whether the radio ﬂaring, or the ejection of new components, precedes or follows the gamma-ray ﬂare

Research Question And Hypothesis
We have recently completed the 5 GHz VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS) of 1127 ﬂat-spectrum sources stronger than 85 mJy in the Northern Cap region Here we make use of the VIPS survey to examine correlations in the parsec-scale jet properties of EGRET blazars All of the well-established trends can be explained by systematically larger Doppler factors in the γ-ray loud blazars We do ﬁnd that the EGRET-detected blazars tend to have higher brightness temperatures, greater core fractions, and possibly larger than average jet opening angles At lower ﬂux levels, radio ﬂux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray ﬂux density

Methodological Details
We have compared the latest EGRET catalog (Hartman et al. 1999) to the recently compiled Combined Radio All-sky Targeted Eight GHz Survey (CRATES) from the intersection compiled a sample of 173 candidate EGRET sources at |b| > 10◦ The VIPS sample (which covers only ∼14% of the sky), is derived from CLASS (Myers et al. 2003) Both CRATES and CLASS include A conﬁguration VLA observations at 8.4 GHz Here we focus on the candidate EGRET sources within the ∼5700 square degree region of the sky covered by VIPS This list contains 12 VIPS sources deemed likely candidates, and 19 VIPS sources deemed plausible candidates A source is considered “likely” if it has FoM > 1, and “plausible” if it has 1.0 > FoM > 0.25 In this section we examine the VLBI-scale properties of the 31 EGRET candidate blazars in this uniform sample for the 25 sources imaged as part of VIPS, we compare them to the properties of the VIPS survey of 1127 sources The classiﬁcation of the EGRET candidates in VIPS is 8 PS (point sources), 3 SJET (short jets), and 14 LJET (long jets) Polarization is detected from all 6 of the MOJAVE sources and from 9 of the 25 VIPS sources for a total of 48 ± 12% This is higher than the average of 36 ± 4% in VIPS overall (Helmboldt et al. 2007a) No k-corrections have been applied, even though the diﬀerence in spectral index between the core and the extended emission will result in a change in the ratio with source redshift The K-S test probability that the two distributions were drawn from the same parent distribution is 4% We have obtained the brightness temperatures from automatic modelﬁts to source components as described in Helmboldt et al. (2007a) For sources with two or fewer components we have further reﬁned the our modelﬁtting procedure by ﬁtting to the visibility data directly The minimum observable size for each source was calculated using equation (2) from Kovalev et al. (2005) we computed the SNR of each core using the core ﬂux density, the rms measured from the 5 GHz image, and a beam FWHM of 3 mas For those sources where the estimated core size is less than this minimum size (∼10% of all VIPS sources), we used the minimum size to compute TB We have measured a mean opening half-angle by the following procedure This is only done for sources with more than 2 total components, (i.e., at least 2 jet components) This means that as in the case of jet bending (see §3.6), we only have quantitative estimates for four of the EGRET/VIPS sources

Procedures And Architectures
VIPS has a ﬂux limit roughly an order of magnitude below the MOJAVE survey and most other samples that have been used to study the properties of EGRET blazars VIPS was carried out between January and August of 2006 and includes 5 GHz, full polarization images of 958 sources as well as 147 total intensity images Over 99% of the VIPS sources have been successfully imaged, with just under 1% being too weak to reliably self-calibrate and image The large, uniform sample provided by VIPS will have many uses, including enabling the intelligent follow-up of gamma-ray blazars GLAST, to be launched in late 2007, will provide a dramatic increase in the resolution and energy range and over two orders of magnitude increase in sensitivity over CGRO-EGRET Applying the same classiﬁcation rules to the 6 MOJAVE sources adds 5 LJET and 1 SJET for totals of 8 (25%) PS, 4 (13%) SJET, and 19 (61%) LJET This can be compared to the population in VIPS as a whole which is 25% PS, 22% SJET, 43% LJET, 9% CSO and 2% CPLX While the number of PS and SJET sources are roughly as expected we ﬁnd a marginally signiﬁcant lack of CSOs, and a marginally signiﬁcant excess of sources with long jets (LJET) The K-S test probability for these two distributions coming from the same parent population is 4% For the jet components (formally, the brightest jet component) the two distributions look fairly similar, except that the spread in the EGRET distribution is smaller the K-S test for this pair of distributions is 11% The opening half-angle measured from each component is then taken to be ψ = arctan[(|y′| + dr)/|x′|] After measuring this for each jet component, we average them to get one value Monte-Carlo simulations of opening angles using the VIPS sample suggests that 3 out of 4 of the randomly sampled values are greater than the median about 30% of the time So, there’s less than a 1 in 3 chance that the EGRET blazars have the same distribution for the opening angle as the whole VIPS sample We see in Figures 2-4 six sources (J08098+5218, J09576+5522, J12215+2813, 1611+343, J16352+3808, J17406+5211) that have opening angles larger than 20 degrees The amount of bending was calculated by ﬁtting a parabola to the centroids of Gaussian model components (Helmboldt et al. 2007b) Looking at the EGRET/MOJAVE and EGRET/VIPS sources by eye only increases the number of highly bent jets by one We see in Figures 2-4 4 sources (J12215+2813, J17226+5856, J17246+6055, J17406+5211) that appear to bend through more than 20 degrees on the parsec scale There does not appear to be an appreciable diﬀerence between the two populations The K-S probability that the two are drawn from the same distribution is 34%

Key Results
At lower ﬂux levels, radio ﬂux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray ﬂux density We do ﬁnd that the EGRET-detected blazars tend to have higher brightness temperatures, greater core fractions, and possibly larger than average jet opening angles A weak correlation is also found with jet length and with polarization The K-S test probability that the two distributions were drawn from the same parent distribution is 4% The core ﬂux density for the EGRET blazars can be found in Table 3 There is some indication that the brightness temperature for the cores of the EGRET candidates may be higher than average The K-S test probability for these two distributions coming from the same parent population is 4% For the jet components (formally, the brightest jet component) the two distributions look fairly similar, except that the spread in the EGRET distribution is smaller the K-S test for this pair of distributions is 11% We see in Figures 2-4 six sources (J08098+5218, J09576+5522, J12215+2813, 1611+343, J16352+3808, J17406+5211) that have opening angles larger than 20 degrees This can be compared to the VIPS images for the survey as a whole which are online Looking at the EGRET/MOJAVE and EGRET/VIPS sources by eye only increases the number of highly bent jets by one We see in Figures 2-4 4 sources (J12215+2813, J17226+5856, J17246+6055, J17406+5211) that appear to bend through more than 20 degrees on the parsec scale There does not appear to be an appreciable diﬀerence between the two populations The K-S probability that the two are drawn from the same distribution is 34% Polarization is detected from all 6 of the MOJAVE sources and from 9 of the 25 VIPS sources for a total of 48 ± 12% This is higher than the average of 36 ± 4% in VIPS overall (Helmboldt et al. 2007a) While the number of PS and SJET sources are roughly as expected we ﬁnd a marginally signiﬁcant lack of CSOs, and a marginally signiﬁcant excess of sources with long jets (LJET) Applying the same classiﬁcation rules to the 6 MOJAVE sources adds 5 LJET and 1 SJET for totals of 8 (25%) PS, 4 (13%) SJET, and 19 (61%) LJET This can be compared to the population in VIPS as a whole which is 25% PS, 22% SJET, 43% LJET, 9% CSO and 2% CPLX

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
From an analysis of the properties of the EGRET candidates in §4, we ﬁnd that candidates tend to have high core fractions and high brightness temperatures These facts support models wherein the gamma-rays are produced in a jet oriented at a small angle to the line-of-sight (e.g., Dermer et al. 1992) The large opening angles seen in 6 out of the 31 sources could also indicate a sight-line close to or within the beaming cone of the radio emission A selection eﬀect of this sort would happen naturally if the gamma rays are more tightly beamed or collimated than the radio In other words, gamma-ray selected sources have higher Doppler factors than the population of compact sources as a whole This can also explain the observations of higher core fractions, higher brightness temperatures, and higher polarization in gamma-ray blazars compared to the population of AGN as a whole as well as the reports of faster motions An unbiased comparison of jet components between the EGRET blazars and the VIPS sample at large supports this, though only 4 of the EGRET/VIPS sources have enough jet components to permit the unbiased (automatic) analysis so the statistics are poor Somewhat more surprising is the evidence in support of long jets, though this is of marginal signiﬁcance Continuing the line of discussion above that EGRET blazars have higher Doppler factors due to small angles to the line-of-sight, the a priori prediction, assuming jets of a ﬁxed length and modest velocity, would be for shorter jets due to projection Obtaining longer jets might be possible if the jets of blazars have intrinsically greater surface brightness, or are highly Doppler boosted compared to sources in radio selected samples Longer jets in blazars could also be obtained if there is a bias in the selection The redshift distribution for the VIPS sample is still incomplete, so it is diﬃcult to investigate possible selection bias at this time Given the weakness of the evidence, especially when comparing the distributions of jet lengths (§3.6), further speculation on this topic is not yet warranted Sources selected on the basis of their γ-ray ﬂux as determined by EGRET appear to have higher Doppler factors than the radio-selected population at large In the VIPS survey this selection manifests itself in larger core fractions, higher core brightness temperatures, increased polarization, and possibly broader jets GLAST, which will launch in late 2007 or early 2008, will detect several thousand (Gehrels & Michelson 1999) of the tens of thousands of compact, radio-loud, ﬂat-spectrum AGN currently known Conﬁrming the tighter beaming angle for the γ-rays should be easily achieved with the improved statistics Therefore it may be advantageous to consider selecting sources with large core fractions, high central brightness temperatures, and large opening angles, as well as strong radio ﬂux density GLAST could also see new populations of AGN including Seyfert galaxies, and low power radio galaxies For this reason it is important to provide contemporaneous ground-based monitoring of a range of source classes, powers, and morphologies Comparisons between the parsec-scale radio structures as revealed by VLBI observations and the time variable γ-ray ﬂux, could discriminate between various models describing the production of the γ-ray emission

Contradictions And Limitations
At lower ﬂux levels, radio ﬂux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray ﬂux density However, in consideration of a larger sample (taken at 2 and 8 GHz) Piner et al. (2007) ﬁnd no signiﬁcant diﬀerence between the jet velocities of EGRET and non-EGRET blazars It still is unclear whether the radio ﬂaring, or the ejection of new components, precedes or follows the gamma-ray ﬂare In some cases multiple VIPS sources are assigned to a single EGRET source Since some EGRET sources may be in fact composites of multiple blazars we have not made any distinction between sources with multiple identiﬁcations and those with a single identiﬁcation The numbers of sources involved are too small to make a deﬁnitive statment Similarly a detailed examination of the polarization properties is handicapped by small number statistics and the fact that we have a mix of 5 GHz measurements for VIPS sources and 15 GHz measurements for MOJAVE sources No k-corrections have been applied, even though the diﬀerence in spectral index between the core and the extended emission will result in a change in the ratio with source redshift Given the similar range in redshifts, and the core dominated nature of the sources, the corrections should be modest and similar for both EGRET-detected blazars and VIPS sources as a whole We see in Figures 2-4 six sources (J08098+5218, J09576+5522, J12215+2813, 1611+343, J16352+3808, J17406+5211) that have opening angles larger than 20 degrees In a few of the blazars the emission is rather diﬀuse which is why they do not show up in the automatic opening angle calculation This means that as in the case of jet bending (see §3.6), we only have quantitative estimates for four of the EGRET/VIPS sources Looking at the EGRET/MOJAVE and EGRET/VIPS sources by eye only increases the number of highly bent jets by one We see in Figures 2-4 4 sources (J12215+2813, J17226+5856, J17246+6055, J17406+5211) that appear to bend through more than 20 degrees on the parsec scale There does not appear to be an appreciable diﬀerence between the two populations The K-S probability that the two are drawn from the same distribution is 34% The redshift distribution for the VIPS sample is still incomplete, so it is diﬃcult to investigate possible selection bias at this time Given the weakness of the evidence, especially when comparing the distributions of jet lengths (§3.6), further speculation on this topic is not yet warranted As we have shown, the gamma-ray ﬂux density is not simply related to the radio ﬂux-density, so selecting the brightest radio sources for study may not maximize the chances of coincidence with strong gamma-ray emission

Claims
EGRET-detected blazars exhibit higher Doppler factors than the general radio-loud population. We do ﬁnd that the EGRET-detected blazars tend to have higher brightness temperatures, greater core fractions, and possibly larger than average jet opening angles All of the well-established trends can be explained by systematically larger Doppler factors in the γ-ray loud blazars Sources selected on the basis of their γ-ray ﬂux as determined by EGRET appear to have higher Doppler factors than the radio-selected population at large However, in consideration of a larger sample (taken at 2 and 8 GHz) Piner et al. (2007) ﬁnd no signiﬁcant diﬀerence between the jet velocities of EGRET and non-EGRET blazars Therefore it may be advantageous to consider selecting sources with large core fractions, high central brightness temperatures, and large opening angles, as well as strong radio ﬂux density
There is no direct correlation between radio flux density and gamma-ray flux density at lower flux levels. At lower ﬂux levels, radio ﬂux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray ﬂux density As we have shown, the gamma-ray ﬂux density is not simply related to the radio ﬂux-density  selecting the brightest radio sources for study may not maximize the chances of coincidence with strong gamma-ray emission

Data And Code Availability
The VIPS images for the survey as a whole which are online

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Monte-Carlo simulations of opening angles using the VIPS sample suggests that 3 out of 4 of the randomly sampled values are greater than the median about 30% of the time

Ethical Considerations
We thank an anonymous referee for constructive suggestions

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 we plot the Gamma-ray mean and peak ﬂuxes against the 8.4 GHz radio ﬂux density from CRATES In Fig. 2 we show the 5 GHz VIPS images or 15 GHz MOJAVE images for all 12 sources identiﬁed with EGRET blazars with high conﬁdence In Figs. 3, and 4 we show the images for 19 sources identiﬁed as plausible counterparts In Fig. 5 we plot the distribution of core-to-jet ratio (deﬁned as the ratio of ﬂux density at 5 GHz in the VLBI core compared to the jet emission from the source at 5 GHz) see distributions in Fig. 6 see lower panel of Fig. 6 see. Fig. 7

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that EGRET-selected blazars possess systematically higher Doppler factors, evidenced by higher core fractions and brightness temperatures 2. The strongest evidence is the 4% K-S test probability indicating the core fraction distribution of EGRET blazars differs significantly from the general VIPS population 3. The future path involves using GLAST to confirm tighter beaming angles and selecting sources based on core fraction rather than just radio flux
